question: Unrealistic CO2 emission rates for coke production and risk of deindustrialisation

The Commission’s proposal to reduce the emission rate for coke production to 0.143 Mg CO2/t is technologically unattainable for European plants. This indicator was calculated statistically, with reference installations’ data not provided, preventing operators from implementing appropriate low-carbon techniques. At the same time, the sector does not receive a sufficient number of allowances, while non-EU coke can circumvent the CBAM mechanism. Given the above: 1.

Will the Commission publish a list of the top 10% of installations that are least carbon intensive on the basis of which the new benchmark was calculated, including details of the processes, raw materials processed and low-carbon technologies used?

How does the Commission reconcile the immediate imposition of these technologically unattainable indicators with the principles of the IED, given the absence of updated BREF documents or BAT conclusions on emissions reductions in the coking sector?

Does the Commission plan to allocate 100 % free emission allowances for coke production or to include it in the CBAM mechanism to prevent the deindustrialisation of the European coke sector and dependence on imports from third countries?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (3.8.2026) The Commission cannot disclose the identity of the installations forming the 10% most efficient group for reasons of business confidentiality surrounding the data. But to increase transparency, the Commission intends to publish a document including benchmark curves and key parameters of the benchmark exercise, as the one published in October 20211.

The benchmark update methodology is set in the EU Emissions Trading System (ETS) Directive2 and is based on the actual performance of the most efficient installations rather than Best Available Techniques conclusions under the Industrial Emissions Directive3, which do not include levels for emissions of greenhouse gases covered by the ETS.
Indeed, the data submitted by the Member States to the Commission of the performance of installations includes verified data on emissions and heat flows, but not feedstock and technology used.

In the case of coke, however, it should be noted that the greenhouse gas intensity of the 10% best-performing installations is lower than the 2026-2030 benchmark level, which indicates that the most efficient installations should still receive sufficient free allocation to cover their emissions.

The Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) review report4 required by the CBAM Regulation5 includes an assessment of a potential extension of CBAM to more goods and precursors based on carbon leakage risk and technical feasibility. Several sectors have been considered in the analytical work, such as organic chemicals and polymers, as highlighted by the Regulation, but also refinery products, among others.
These materials have been prioritised for further assessment. It is therefore too early to say whether coke would be included in any future CBAM scope extension.
